items.body: A veteran of groundbreaking music-video and visual collaborations, Ben Stokes puts his most personal stamp on Dimensional Holophonic Sound (DHS), his singular project blending acid electronics, old-school analog imagery, and experimental video production. Simultaneously, Stokes has built a distinctive career at the intersection of sound, art, technology, and visuals. Inside Ben Stokes’ vinyl obsession Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound   Benjamin Stokes could exist solely as a collaborator with other artists and his resume would remain an envious one. He has directed music videos for giants like Nine Inch Nails, Public Enemy, Ministry, The Orb and Meat Beat Manifesto, the latter of which he’s also a band member alongside industrial dance music pioneer Jack Dangers, whom Stokes additionally collaborates with in another outfit called Man From Mantis. He has created visuals for DJ Shadow‘s live sets, directed hype video for the Dallas Cowboys, and even helped pull off the feat of M.I.A. and Janelle Monae performing as holograms at each other’s live shows, simultaneously, on opposite coasts of the United States. And this is only a small scratch on his winning lottery ticket of collaborations. Dimensional Holofonic Sound (DHS) however, is singularly Ben Stokes. “I love collaborating with people but I think every artist needs a solo project,” he says. “Something that is their own signature and unique flavor.” I spoke with Stokes—ironically as he took a break from creating visuals for DJ Shadow‘s upcoming Endtroducing 30th Anniversary tour—to talk about his new DHS album, Concept Record, AI art, love of acid music, and any upcoming plans for live shows. “[Concept Record] is kind of like a big love letter to vinyl itself,” says Stokes. “I mean, the concept is, ‘The record is the concept.’ It’s all about vinyl. It’s an art object. I went to art school and I was trained to make objects, so it was very important to me.” That love of records is so grand that he took a risk, spent the extra money on the bells and whistles—including fifteen lock-groove loop tracks—and wrote his love letter on a hand-crafted double-vinyl edition of the album engineered with Anne-Marie Suenram of Suenram Productions in San Pablo, California, the only woman-owned and operated cutting and mastering company of its kind in North America. Ben Stokes and Anne-Marie Suenram engineering the lacquer cut for the vinyl edition of Concept Record. Taken from Stokes’ Instagram page. Locking into the groove :: Cutting the vinyl with its special features was a true labor of love. “It was indeed a major learning experience that challenged me to apply everything I’d learned,” Suenram says via email, “but with Ben‘s encouragement I was able to figure out what I needed to do. Ben‘s record was, and still is, the only record I’ve done with this kind of cut,” she says. “I wanted to try to do all the kind of physical, fun things that you can do only with vinyl,” Stokes continues, “like lock-grooves, beat matching and putting things at 133.33 beats per minute, which if you look at those tracks that are at that tempo, the grooves on the physical record actually kind of line up in an interesting visual way. And um, little side note, the inner disk labels, if you set your phone to 30 frames a second [and record a video] you get some semblance of a little animation there.” Honing in specifically on the logistics of creating a record with so many lock-groove tracks, Stokes brought along a favorite record from his collection called 500 Lock-Grooves By 500 Artists as a template. “Anywhere you drop the needle, it locks. [Suenram] looked at that record under a microscope and she was like, ‘I’m not sure how they did this, and we can’t do it quite this way with my machinery,'” Stokes explains. “The workaround was to create sort of like an entry ramp onto a freeway,” he says, “so there’s a little silence before each lock groove, and then it locks. It circles in on itself. And you really can’t test it, so you don’t really know if it’s going to work until you get your test pressings and at that point, I was like, well, I’m not going back.” Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound   Signature Ben Stokes kind of stuff :: Lucky for him, as well as for us, it worked very well and serves as another feature of the record’s concept, which is mixing the two records with each other—or with other records—on turntables. Stokes has done DJ sets with the album already, using his 500 Lock-Grooves record alongside Concept Record, and says they worked perfectly together. “Every lock groove on any record will match up with any lock groove on any other record, if you’re playing at the same speed.” He encourages musicians and DJs to post their own mixes to Instagram. “I would love to see what people do,” he says excitedly. All of these nifty features would be mere window dressing without solid DHS music at the core. “I didn’t want it to overshadow that it’s also a new DHS record,” says Stokes. “Part of it came about because I stumbled into a really funny sample, and it’s basically like [a celebrity] interviewing himself, and he’s talking about his album, and he’s like, ‘Oh, it’s just a great album. I mean, it’s what they call a concept record.’ So, that kind of sent me in that trajectory… led me down a rabbit hole. After that initial, like, kind of inspiration, then I just threw in every sample that I have of people talking about records. It’s got some acid house tracks and some minimal electronic-y stuff. I don’t know, signature Ben Stokes kind of stuff.” A good portion of Concept Record is dedicated to the acid music style DHS is known for. From dropping the “Green Acid” and subsequently being treated in the “Hospital Tent,” to the reminder of “I Can Feel It,” blooping along with “Supersonic Holofonic,” then flashing back with “Cut To Black” and “Full Blackout,” the whole middle section plays like one big, aural, acid-trip. “Yeah, there is kind of like a little storyline there,” admits Stokes. When asked what draws him to the style, he replies, “It was seminal. I went to school in Chicago in 1986, and the whole house thing was just teetering into acid. I don’t even think the term acid in 1986 was prevalent. But I was schooled on that stuff through WBMX radio in Chicago where, literally, I mean, the entire city would be listening to the same station. You’d hear it coming out of cars. On your front stoop, you’d hear it, one car going by with the Doppler effect, and you’d hear another one on the same station come in the other direction. I mean, it was just such a magical time. I was so young and that music was just totally new and unlike anything else that I had ever heard. I already loved electronic stuff, but this was just like, wow, these endless mixes of pretty much anonymous stuff WBMX would play for 4 hours on Friday and Saturday night. So that was just a really formative time for me. Definitely a really cool time, I think, for music.”   Redefining The Concept Record :: Now 40 years removed from those halcyon college days, the imagery Stokes has created for Concept Record‘s gatefold cover is decidedly 2026. While the content of many of the pictures may evoke the 1950s and 1960s in style, the artificial intelligence used to create them, as well as the music video for the album’s title track, “Concept Record​,” is apparent. “I actually hate AI,” Stokes says. “If I had found some film about a company that made a shiny silver record and everyone was analyzing it, I’m sure I would have used that.” He underscores that working in the industry he’s in, often being called in by companies as an art director for audio/visual projects, “You gotta keep up with the new tools. I spent a year just learning how to use some of the AI tools.” For Stokes it’s a reflection of this moment in time, yet he still tried to approach it from a familiar standpoint. “In a lot of ways, these images for the cover and for that video were very much like creating stock footage from possibly old educational films or something like that. I just created them in a very different way,” he says. “But it felt kind of familiar territory for me because I was thinking of it like stock footage.” Don’t expect AI creation to be the new norm for Stokes though. “You mentioned the ‘Supersonic [Holofonic]’ video,” he says, which I indeed had. “Well, that’s all found-footage. That’s very DHS.” He continues, “I’m sure that I will use [AI] again for work things, but when it comes to DHS stuff I think I’m going old school for everything going forward. It was an interesting detour and I feel like that’s something that, as an artist, I do often,” he says. “I did that video, I did this album cover, and then I canceled all my subscriptions. I’m going back to my roots. I like going outside with my camera and shooting stuff or doing stop motion animation. And I think that people are kind of probably craving a little bit more rough-around-the-edges analog look, you know?” Stokes stresses as to the musical content, “I did put a very big disclaimer on the inside that no audio was created using AI.”   The Art of the Tease :: With Concept Record being Ben Stokes‘ ode to the vinyl record, it almost begs the question as to what he’s been spinning lately. “I’ve been really getting into 45s,” he says. “I go up to my mom’s cabin in northern Minnesota and there’s like this thrift store called Rick’s Relics in Tower, Minnesota, and they just have this phenomenal collection of records. Just boxes and boxes and piles that, you know, they’re all out of their sleeves. It’s like 25 cents for a 7-inch. And I’ve been picking up all kinds, like The Trashmen, a Minneapolis band from the 60s. They’re, like, garage surf sort of style. I love a lot of that shit.” In continuing to answer the same question, Stokes pivots to Meat Beat Manifesto. “I absolutely love everything Jack [Dangers] does. I think it’s just incredible.” He admits to a little name dropping on his album. “I had to name-call Meat Beat Manifesto by naming a song, “Meat Beat Manifesto Soundcheck.” That was us at a show, doing soundcheck for a show.” Casually in the conversation Stokes drops a bombshell: “There is going to be a Meat Beat Manifesto tour early next year.” Cue the sound of a needle scratching across a record. “We’re booked to do a couple shows in Europe, and then there’s going to be some dates here [in the U.S.]. And, um, more info to come! And at some point, Jack and I are going to do probably a [Man From] Mantis album. Sometime in the, uh, indefinite future,” he teases. Does this mean new Meat Beat material is around the corner? “Yeah, well, Jack‘s always, always got new stuff coming out,” is the response. What of a DHS live tour supporting Concept Record though? “Well, I would love to,” says Stokes. “I’m trying to figure out a stealthy version that I can fit in the trunk of my car and like, you know, do at least a small mini tour. LA, I think, is pretty conceivable. And of course, when we do shows locally here in San Francisco, I get the absolute pleasure of having Jack performing with me as DHS.” You might guess what Stokes offers next: “I’m just going to have to keep you posted on that.” Perhaps Ben Stokes just came up with his next concept: The Art of the Tease. If so, it’s coming along nicely. Concept Record is available on Bandcamp. Concept Record by Dimensional Holofonic Sound    The post Chit Chat with Ben Stokes of Dimensional Holofonic Sound first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: From its roots as a music blog to a fiercely independent label built around physical releases, Somewherecold Records has grown from Jason Lamoreaux’s love of experimental music into a deeply personal effort to give artists and their work something lasting to hold onto. There’s (still) a chill in the air… Déka by The Corrupting Sea   When did Somewherecold Records start, and what was your inspiration? Jason Lamoreaux :: The original version of the label was a partnership with another label in Texas. I think we put out 8 or so albums with them. In 2008, the blog shut down for really accidental reasons and I wanted to start it back up again in 2016. Part of the initiative was the fact that I started to record under The Corrupting Sea and wanted to put my own music out because I thought no one else would care (I’m glad I was very wrong). Anyway, I was a shoegaze DJ at the time and ran into The Beremy Jet‘s EPs but they had no physical release. For me, digital only is a travesty for many albums. I’m very much a physical media person because the entire package is the album. I love putting artwork together, getting the right combination of packaging, and offering the world something to actually hold. Perhaps that’s the Gen Xer in me but I can’t get beyond it really. So, once The Beremy Jets was on board, I began reaching out to folks I had interviewed or reviewed or I was a fan of and brought some into the label. As of now, the roster has been whittled down extensively due to money, health issues, and just the world in general seeming to reject art (perhaps out of financial desperation or something other). At the end of the day, I just want to leave something beautiful behind in this world. The structure of the label is very much inspired by Daniel Miller and the early Mute Records approach to artists. He did it right with honor. He can sleep at night while I don’t know how other record label CEOs can (I’m speaking primarily about major labels that rip off their artists). Anyway, That’s the short of it. Who were some of your initial artist relations, and did your location help or hinder progress? Jason Lamoreaux :: I started the label while living in Texas. I hadn’t gotten to the point where I wanted to play live or even had figured out how to do so with what I was putting together. The location however was great because there are so many experimental artists in Dallas and Austin and getting to cut my teeth live in those places was a huge challenge and inspiration. I didn’t get any on the label till later for some reason, but the label was young and others had different outlets. Initial artists included Aidan Baker, Ummagma, Mis+ress, Yellow6, Niev, Zombie Girlfriend, Thee Koukouvaya, Winterwood, and then my projects like The Corrupting Sea, The Warm Jets, and more came later. I think I’ve worked with around 50 artists over the years. What were some challenges of starting the label, and how did you envision it standing apart? Jason Lamoreaux :: I’m not sure how to answer this except the Somewherecold reputation was well received in the music world because we did a lot of work on interviews and reviews between 2000-2008. I initially started the blog up again with interviews from God is an Astronaut and The Album Leaf but the label side of things started to overwhelm and I decided to move in that direction for the time being. The label is curated by me and I guess that’s the thread through the label. Walls of sound, intimate ambience, electronic experimental, cowboy drone, and other genres are, for me, deeply connected and I wanted the label to reflect my love for those things. Further, I’m an artist. I wanted to be an artist available to other artists. It felt like purpose and, in many ways, still does. What is your motivation in keeping the label moving forward into the next decade? Jason Lamoreaux :: This is a constant question in the back of my mind. I would love for it take off and people to actually support it in full. We don’t press very many physical copies but the current landscape makes it almost impossible to sell out it seems. There is a lot of noise out there, too many algorithms, and a ton of cynicism. So, in my mind, I’m taking it year by year. Once it becomes too onerous, I will likely walk away and maybe keep me and a few collective artists to keep it going. But, for now, we stay the course. That said, Elasticstage in the UK has made it possible to release so much music on vinyl and CDs over on the European side of things. My first 10 The Corrupting Sea albums are now up for order there as well as all the new releases for the label. It’s a press on demand site and the products are beautiful and sound great. The shipping is very low if you order 3 items (their limite right now per order) at a time. “There is a lot of noise out there, too many algorithms, and a ton of cynicism. So, in my mind, I’m taking it year by year.” ~Jason Lamoureaux How do you deliver the label’s “sound” to listeners and fans (through distribution, campaigns, live shows, word of mouth, etc.)? Jason Lamoreaux :: There are a number of ways. I have a rather large promo email system but that is also an issue since so many get inundated with requests for review, etc (I know you probably get the same). The label does have distribution through The Business in Anacortes, Washington. The place is run by this amazing couple and I wish folks would use them more. Again, getting above the noise as it were. Most of my artists play live but I don’t see that as a deal breaker. A Journey of Giraffes is a studio project and has been so well received. Others are new and I’m not sure if they will play live or not. Again, not a deal breaker. I think people can enjoy music outside of the live world especially considering how terrible support for local artists has become in those live spaces. In terms of word of mouth, well, the silence can be deafening. As a label owner, you often have no idea what fans are thinking, if the label is being well received, or artists being listened to until you bump into someone who tells you differently. You would think that with the mountain of communication options, you would hear things. But you don’t and it can get quite lonely. I do post on social media but I’m beginning to see it as a hindrance rather than a plus. The label is heavily pro-lgbtq+, anti-war, pro-immigrants, and more. The people who run these sites have proven to be otherwise and it’s becoming more and more difficult to justify any presence on Social Media. At this moment, plans are being sorted to go to a singular website with Bandcamp attached and nothing more. Lastly, I have uploaded to streaming, which, financially, is a joke. Does it capture people’s attention? I have no idea. You have to have so many streams even to make a penny. I’m behind on those uploads but the label is in a moment of organization and I’ll be uploading past albums that I’ve missed due to daily life. For me, streaming is not a priority. For the same reasons I dislike social media, I dislike streaming companies even more. Spotify, for me, is now a no go. I refuse to place my own music up there but my other artists are welcome to on their own. I don’t control their music. The Déka box set is encased in a purple velvet box set. It contains the first 10 albums remastered by Jason T. Lamoreaux. All come in artwork matching the box. Also, each album except for Ontology has a brand new track attached as a hidden track. items.body: Rather than treating glitch as surface decoration, Signal_Black builds an entire skeletal language around it. What emerges is a unified, tightly constructed collection of focused (yet splintered) electronics—one that pushes exploratory sound forward through distortion, fragmentation, and a distinctly futuristic sense of movement. A distinctly futuristic sense of movement Revealed several months ago in April 2026, this sleek eight-piece suite (titled Disruptive Event) still carries a sense of propulsion and precise direction. From its opening moments, Signal_Black (aka Marcin) establishes a dense exchange between analog glitch and Autechre-influenced sound-design, immediately evident on “Higher Ground.” From there, the project descends deep below terra firma, evolving through scraped emotive melodic fragments and moving further into ambient-industrial IDM abstraction. A fixation on roughened rhythms and microscopic melodic fibers gives “Internal Merge” its distinctive tension, folding broken structures into looping forms that gradually become cohesive without losing their instability. “Long Now” shifts toward wobbling bass pressure, while “TON” sinks into darker ambient territory, and what becomes more evident is that each track extends the artist’s interest in malfunction, texture, and controlled disorientation. As the final pieces move through old-school Arovane-like finesse, especially on “Text of The Present,” “Chronic” delivers a more microscopic form of sonic deformation. Its fractured detail reflects the album’s central idea: a disruptive event capable of interrupting established operations, routines, or systems. Rather than treating glitch as surface decoration, Signal_Black builds an entire skeletal language around it. What emerges is a unified, tightly constructed collection of focused (yet splintered) electronics—one that pushes exploratory sound forward through distortion, fragmentation, and a distinctly futuristic sense of movement. While Disruptive Event channels our favored old-school IDM mechanics associated with Richard Devine, Gescom, Funckarma, Alva Noto, SND, and Funkstörung, Signal_Black takes that lineage somewhere altogether stranger—refining tone, deepening texture, and redirecting momentum into a galaxy of its own. items.body: That exchange between past and present is central to Axial Opposition. Classic Multiplex structures remain recognizable, yet the melodic synthesis gives them renewed dimension, allowing vintage electronic language to exist alongside contemporary detail. A duo creating electronics with melody as its backbone [PCLLP 037] Axial Opposition by Multiplex   Multiplex are brothers Christian and Roland Dormon, their focused frenzy of pulsating electronics sees no barriers, but always anchored by a deep melodic instinct. Emerging from IDM’s early days more than two decades ago—recall their releases with Toytronic, Senton, Piehead, and U-Cover)— they now find a home with Belarus-based People Can Listen following recent releases Colour Kinetica (Bricolage) and Human, I Love You (w/ Remixes) (Clean Error). Their historical relevance remains an important factoid for anyone new to sandblasted, ever-veering strains of broken beats, IDM, and melodic electro, yet beneath those fractured forms is where Multiplex have always been most distinctive: tuneful synthesis, layered with ambient propulsion and shaped into electronic structures that feel both precise and uniquely alive. Axial Opposition opens with punishing electro, eerily transcendental in its summation of the 42-second opener “Reality (Interlude),” before settling into their bread-and-butter language of pristine melodies, glowing synth lines, and carefully interlocked sound design textures. Synthesizers are not simply used as rhythmic machinery here; they carry the emotional weight, allowing melodies to drift, repeat, fracture, and return with a nostalgic clarity. That sensibility comes to life across favorites such as “In Your Dreams,” “Pulsar Energy,” “Verhn,” “Aditya,” and “Neeta_x,” before dissolving into the closing atmospheric layers of “Implode (outro).” “What makes the collection compelling is how naturally those eras communicate: older synth ideas are not merely revived, but repolished, expanded, and brought into the present without losing their original character.” ~Pietro Da Sacco With 24 years now behind Pinghaus Frequencies (Toytronic), alongside earlier productions dating to 1999, Multiplex have long signalled a duo creating electronics with melody as its backbone. Axial Opposition gathers new and vintage material after more than 15 years of silence, sending music back and forth between studios, adding elements along the way and shaping everything into a final mix. What makes the collection compelling is how naturally those eras communicate: older synth ideas are not merely revived, but repolished, expanded, and brought into the present without losing their original character. That exchange between past and present is central to Axial Opposition. Classic Multiplex structures remain recognizable, yet the melodic synthesis gives them renewed dimension, allowing vintage electronic language to exist alongside contemporary detail. There is nostalgia here, but it never feels archival; sounds that might have belonged to another era are given fresh circuitry, fresh atmosphere, and a new context. After such a long silence, Multiplex return not by abandoning what made their sound distinctive, but by reconnecting with it and pushing it forward. A multiverse of melodic electronics, where old synthesis is made new again, and one that only Multiplex can navigate so well. Axial Opposition is available on People Can Listen. items.body: What makes Headphone Beats 2025-2026 so exciting is that it never settles into its own language. Every time you think you’ve identified the rules, it quietly moves the goalposts. Genres are treated less as destinations than as raw materials: broken apart, stretched, folded, obscured and rebuilt into strange new functional objects. Moments of tenderness appear inside the delicate violence Headphone Beats 2025-2026 by Winter Back   South Korea’s Wona returns in a different spacesuit with Headphone Beats 2025-2026 by Winter Back, an album that feels less like a collection of tracks than a future archetype: a visceral, crystal-clear demonstration of what electronic sound work can become when technique, instinct and design aesthetics are allowed to mutate together. I’d hazard a guess it was made through a pair of headphones over the course of a year, because there’s something intensely close-up about it—and the title proposed, eh? On the surface, you might identify glitch aesthetics, but that’s only the doorway. Beneath it are drill and trap rhythms, tensile funk, lo-fi breakbeat trippery, obfuscation, drops, crescendos, proto-brass, rolling bass and complex and simple synthesis that seems perpetually on the verge of becoming something else. I’m genuinely thrilled this landed on my figurative desk. It’s remorselessly stunning. “Matmat” has my heart: thunderous, rolling beats tumble around each other in waterfalls of hugeness and electrification while the low end holds you prisoner. “AGN” stinks—in the very best sense. Its half-time stutter is a screwface anthem of dropping beat and bass pulse, scratch-and-tear music so filthy you can almost smell it. Backward melodies emerge from the darkness to lighten the load, moments of tenderness appearing inside the delicate violence. “There is beauty in the abrasion and an almost ridiculous confidence in allowing sounds to seem to remain unresolved.” ~Will Wonks And this is the crucial distinction: this isn’t impenetrable sound design made to impress other sound designers. It’s a highly informed, deeply nuanced deviance in sound, rhythm and strata. Our title track “Winter Back” demonstrates an enviable approach to drum programming before its apparent mid-point collapse detonates into a spanking groove of epic proportions—the holy grail of contemporary electronic funk. “TLD” may contain the most outrageous break on the record, somehow folding rhythm back into itself and emerging as something entirely new: a funky drummer for 3026. Nearly every track appears to reach a point where it dissolves, sheds its skin and reconstitutes somewhere else. These aren’t conventional breakdowns so much as dimensional ruptures. “Bedrop” is the perfect example: atmosphere and tense pads briefly suspend the album in mid-air before the future-klaxon begins its nagging ascent and the whole thing lurches forward again. “Set Jen” brings tribal toms and deranged circus bells into some kind of beautifully unstable agreement. “Dedication” removes the floor entirely, a beatless blast of aural oxygen that makes the subsequent savagery hit harder. “Starb” and “Still Ago” sound like saucepans being thrown down the stairs through a malfunctioning computer, grinding the listener into submission, before “220” closes the circuit with single hi-hits, elastic wubs and a sense of space suddenly expanding beyond the edges of the record. What makes Headphone Beats 2025-2026 so exciting is that it never settles into its own language. Every time you think you’ve identified the rules, it quietly moves the goalposts. Genres are treated less as destinations than as raw materials: broken apart, stretched, folded, obscured and rebuilt into strange new functional objects. There is beauty in the abrasion and an almost ridiculous confidence in allowing sounds to seem to remain unresolved. It feels experimental without announcing itself as experimental. It feels futuristic without resorting to the usual sci-fi vocabulary. Most importantly, it feels alive. It’s a great example of electronic music one would want to spend time inside, not simply consume. The deeper you go, the more its internal architecture reveals itself: tiny rhythmic decisions, concealed transitions, unexpected pockets of funk, bass frequencies that seem to have their own gravitational field. It rewards repeated listening because it keeps changing shape under examination. You don’t exhaust it; you develop a better understanding of how much is actually happening. A genuinely extraordinary piece of work. A 10/10 proposition where nothing is missing and nothing needs adding. Rare. Welcomed. Headphone Beats 2025-2026 is available on SoundSupply_Service. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Frank Zappa's "pastiche" technique had taken on a new immediacy and a breakneck pace starting with Over-Nite Sensation, when Ian Underwood (saxophones and flute) joined Sal Marquez (trumpet) and George Duke (keyboards) and, notably, this marked the first time Jean-Luc Ponty was a member of his regular band (which included musicians from the Mothers of Invention alongside the Big-Band lineup that began with Waka/Jawaka). With the follow-up album, Apostrophe ('), the music went a step further compositionally, reformulating genres through Zappa's unique stamp combined with the contributions of the virtuoso group he had surrounded himself with.In "Don't Eat the Yellow Snow," he sang rapidly and the band played at a fast pace, except when they shifted the rhythm for comedic effect. This embodied the Dadaist approach that defined his music and his deconstruction of familiar forms, an approach that could lead to paradoxes, such as in "Nanook Rubs It," where he tackled jazz by singing in the style of Tom Waits's spoken-word delivery, ironically, after Waits himself had served as his opening act in the early 70s and struggled to win over the audience. There was psychedelia interwoven with soul, yet nothing quite like what we knew; the backing vocals contributed significantly to the band's sound, a sound truly unfathomable within the Zappa universe.Atonal music, specifically the contemporary classical style of Schoenberg and Var�se (the very same artist to whom Chicago dedicated their track "A Hit by Var�se") could be seen distilled within "St. Alfonzo's Pancake Breakfast." This represented a challenging exercise in synthesizing that entire musical world, an approach he would explore in greater depth years later on one of his masterpieces, One Size Fits All."Father O'Blivion" is a jazz-rock track that shifts into cosmic and progressive territory with effortless ease, a mere turn of a few notes, always possessing that knack for making highly complex music sound deceptively simple. "Cosmik Debris" was a blend of blues and soul, punctuated and interwoven by the invisible, precise stitches of Ruth Underwood's percussion. Zappa adopted a highly suggestive Barry White-esque persona, yet his guitar playing was raw, wild, and distorted; one could never predict where a solo or a riff might lead. He was truly many figures rolled into one: singer, guitarist, composer, and, of course, orchestra conductor."Excentrifugal Forz" speaks for itself right from the title, highlighting the force that emanated from his music during that era, a time when even rock was an indivisible whole. The same can be said for the track "Apostrophe", featuring Jack Bruce on bass, which sounds dense, powerful, and heavy; it emerged from an unexpected jam session and was captured that way forever. The bass and guitar tones of Zappa and Bruce meshed perfectly, creating a contrast that thrived within the stereo mix. It is a tour-de-force, especially considering how the wild playing styles of McLaughlin and Zappa represent such vastly different extremes."Uncle Remus" provided a fantastic counterpoint at this stage of the �lbum, a sort of veiled tribute to Dr. John, featuring New Orleans-style gospel and rhythm & blues courtesy of George Duke. Stink-Foot had a distinctive way of recording the instruments, incorporating echoes, shifts in mood and atmosphere, and killer guitar solos that, much like the electric keyboard, would break into that jazzy-blues vibe.Apostrophe (') is the crucial link that, following Over-Nite Sensation, would give rise to One Size Fits All; it stands out by showcasing Zappa's signature style, transforming what was essentially a deconstructed transitional period into a distinct era in its own right.

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — Funny how a riff can sound modern, but I guess that's the way it works. Music moves in waves. This album feels very grabby, fresh and now. It's intricately constructed and great-sounding, ready to put any serious home stereo to the test.Where to start? The singing, where this band excels... and that groove! The drums are as much about rhythm as they are about texture. There's plenty of satisfying, head-bang-able metal riffing, paired tightly with great bass work. I'm reminded at times of classic Smashing Pumpkins, so there must be some grunge influence in there as well.The multilayered male/female vocals is a very alluring part of the PRR sound. Their voices don't just blend; they're sculpted together, fused and purposely locked in?creating more of a Beach Boys vibe than casually tagged-on harmonies.There are some definite Pink Floyd-inspired moments here too, particularly in the 12 minute title track 'Terrifying Angels". Then again, maybe I've got it backwards, the PRR take on it could inspire Pink Floyd. Time will tell, but on first listen, I felt I was listening to a masterpiece of modern progressive rock unfold before my ears. It clears out all the cobwebs of stereotypical prog epics and treads boldly into new cinematic textures and possibilities."Terrifying Angels" is a pretty jarring topic to tackle, so it's probably not going to be the "light" entry in the PRR catalogue. And while there's plenty of complexity and detail here, there's also lots of breathing room. But don't get too comfortable in those quieter passages, there's usually some musical surprise waiting around the next corner.Often the song structure seems indecipherable, dragging you at times through room after room of emotional spaces. I love how the familiar can suddenly become strange and new. The lyrics feel important simply because of the way the vocalists are emoting themAnd a shout-out to "Below Radiance," which really shows off Bruce Soord's skills as a mixer, managing all those incredible, epic synth textures without letting the whole thing turn into sonic soup.The last track, "Hold Your Wrath," is 15 minutes long but is a different kind of beast, not an attempt at the epic in a grand way, but a more understated, meditative journey. It features delicate, beautiful, intimate guitar parts, some wonderfully creative drum work, and I love that electronic bass. It feels like another experimental track for the band, though really, the whole album feels adventurous. And despite all of this, you can still bounce to this band.Prog dog score is 4.5 out of 5 dog bones, or 4 out of 5 for the progarchives system.

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — This is actually a divisive album among devoted Yes fans, mainly because of the absence of key founding member and vocalist Jon Anderson. Gone was his distinct and immediately recognizable high tenor voice, along with the more fanciful and fantasy-like lyrics that had become part of the Yes sound. For others, it may be the departure of keyboardist Rick Wakeman that makes Drama difficult to embrace. Filling his shoes was Geoff Downes, whose keyboard approach was quite different from Wakeman's. Although Downes had considerable classical training, his work on Drama placed greater emphasis on texture, tone and the emerging possibilities of synthesizers and electronic technology, bringing some of the new-wave sensibilities of the Buggles into Yes.I recall that sometime around 1980, or perhaps early 1981, my brother and I had each picked up another Yes album. I got Tormato; he got Drama. Neither of us, as very new Yes fans at the time, realized that Jon Anderson wasn't on Drama. Instead, Trevor Horn, known for his work with the Buggles, had stepped into Anderson's shoes.My brother asked if I wanted to trade. I don't remember whether I agreed or not'I liked both albums equally. If I had based the trade strictly on the album artwork, though, Drama would have won hands down. It's one of Roger Dean's great Yes covers.One of the great tracks on this important album is the opening epic 'Machine Messiah.' For anyone who had become a fan of Steve Howe's guitar work and direction on Tormato, this must have been something of a shock. As the track begins Howe goes all-in on the heavy, riff-driven guitar sound here, venturing into territory that sounds like an early precursor to prog-metal. Not that he hadn't demonstrated an aggressive side before, with tracks such as 'The Gates of Delirium,' 'Close to the Edge,' 'Heart of the Sunrise,' and 'Perpetual Change.' But this was different'a heavier, more metallic approach that, in retrospect, foreshadowed the emergence of that off-shoot of prog-rock.The track changes its palette several times, at one point featuring tentative acoustic guitar and an epic, almost devotional or cultish atmosphere as technology is worshipped and revered. It feels surprisingly prescient today. Another major section is full of hope, though, as Horn reaches for notes his vocal cords could barely have been expected to reach: 'Maybe we'll change / Offered the chance / To finally unlearn our lessons and alter our stance.' 'Man in a White Car' is a little ditty that I wish they had developed into a full-grown song. Instead, it serves nicely as a palette cleanser after the frighteningly epic 'Machine Messiah,' which sounds like it could easily have drawn lightning bolts down from the sky.'Does It Really Happen' features one of Chris Squire's all-time hookiest bass lines. Alan White's sheer power and focus as a drummer is especially potent throughout this album, on this track as on any on Drama. The drums and bass feed off each other with near-ferocity, while the vocals are equally aggressive. Squire's distinctive voice shines through on this one, while Horn's singing is also well showcased. Together, they form something of a power duo.The new-wave vibes are prominent in the opening melodic instrumental section, but there are hints of Yes' Going for the One too, thanks to Steve Howe's distorted pedal steel, with his steel bar swooping between the chords.'Into the Lens' is the oft-overshadowed track on this album, despite showcasing the band's hyper-creativity. Horn provides some more emotional and introspective vocals, with lyrics that seem to explore detachment and observation. Once again, Downes' synths transport Yes firmly into new-wave territory, while the song still holds onto its proggy identity through its numerous passages and sections. There's even a wonderfully eclectic mix of sounds, including sitar and vocoder. Howe also leans into his 'talking guitar' sound, using a wah-wah pedal to make the instrument seem to speak.'Run Through the Light' is a rare and daring track for Yes, featuring Trevor Horn on fretless bass while Squire instead plays some affected piano chords around the track. Horn's vocals add a completely new sound for Yes, with a staccato, almost stuttering effect. It seems likely Squire was coaching Horn through the track, and there's a story that by having Horn play bass, the song was more likely to make the final album cut'something Squire seemed quite determined to ensure.'Tempus Fugit' is a muscular song. Chris Squire provides the fast, heavy bass riffs that hold the whole thing together like the bones of a roller coaster. There's also some early use of the Fairlight CMI in the 'yes, yes, yes, yes' synthetic vocal samples at the end. It's an amusing little break in the fourth wall, with Yes seemingly making a self-conscious reference to itself. I can attest to how effective it was: my first conscious exposure to Yes was hearing this song on the radio, and that repeated 'yes, yes, yes, yes' stuck in my head. After running downstairs to tell my brother about this new band I had discovered, I would soon be buying my first Yes records. Ironically, Drama was one of the last Yes albums my brother and I actually bought in around 1980. This is not Yes's best record, but it is essential nonetheless, chock full of exciting music, and everyone in the band sounds fresh and revitalized. I give it a 4.75 out of 5 dog bones. (5 for prog archives round-ed off score)

There is a bit of experimentation going on as well,particularly in the rhythm section, as drummer Martin Lopez lays down some diverse and delightfulgrooves, perhaps channeling his inner Danny Carey. The vocals represent another interesting part ofthis record, as the delivery of Joel Ekel�f is warm and emotive, definitely befitting the etherealstyle of rock that prevails on 'Tellurian'. Thiscompletely takes away their compositional edge, and it also diminishes the appeal of the strongertracks. Therefore, 'Tellurian' is hardly a groundbreaking prog metal masterpiece; it is more of adriven and consistent collection of songs, which salvages the weaker moments, and presents Soen as agroup searching for a recognizable sound.

An album that has Queenand Skrillex as major influences is meant to be compositionally intense and stylistically chaotic,which is precisely what 'The 2nd Law' is - a collection of epic, theatrical, and electronic-riddenpop rock anthems that broadly explore the concepts of authoritarianism, power-control dynamics aswell as conspiracy and fiction. A fascinating mixture of disparate styles is at stake here, as theband offers an entertaining collection informed by past releases like 'The Resistance', but leaningmore into the artsy electronic side of their music. However, with its thirteen tracks, 'The 2nd Law'is hardly the most consistent release from the British trio. The futuristic production stylehighlights the strong melodies on tracks like 'Animals' and 'Save Me', but it also renders some ofthe mellower songs utterly dull.The stark contrasts between the funky dance pop elements, the hammering rock riffs, the energeticdubstep beats, and the operatic vocal experiments, however, make 'The 2nd Law' somewhat of aschizophrenic listen. The two closing pieces are quite interesting as well, despite being mostly instrumentaland vastly dubstep-inspired. I still think the use of electronics and digital instruments on thisalbum is one of its stronger features, but the overall mixture of genres and dynamics can easilybecome overwhelming. I would not call 'The 2nd Law' a classic but I definitely feel it is the kindof record only Muse could attempt to produce.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — *Here Comes the Rain* is most likely the final album by Magnum, a British hard rock band formed in 1972, with 25 studio albums to its credit if you count the two albums released in 1997 and 1999 under the name Hard Rain. With about ten tracks per album, that brings the total to around 250 songs, almost all of which were composed by guitarist Tony Clarkin (he only let Russ Ballard help him with a few minor tracks on the 1990 album *Goodnight L.A.*). This simple calculation highlights just how prolific a songwriter Clarkin was?a rarity in this field. I wrote "was" because Tony suddenly passed away in early January 2024, four days before the release of this quasi-posthumous album.Beyond the context of this tragic event, dedicating a few lines to Magnum in a French magazine devoted to progressive music?even in the broadest sense?is debatable. It's true that aside from the first two albums, *Kingdom of Madness* (1978) and *Magnum II* (1979)?to which one might possibly add the less simplistic half of *The Eleventh Hour* (1983) and *On a Storyteller's Night* (1985)? four highly recommended albums in which the British band seemed to put their own spin on the American formula for full-bodied pop-prog that Styx and Boston had devised with the success we all know, the rest of Magnum's discography offered nothing more than yet another high-energy AOR album.Carefully crafted melodies, a rigid structure that very often followed the verse/chorus/verse/bridge/chorus pattern, and tight, driving rhythms?all of this was far from enough for an audience seeking progressive musical brilliance, despite the regular inclusion on each album of one or two more adventurous tracks with slightly more complex structures.Since the arrival of keyboardist Rick Benton in 2018 (replacing Mark Stanway), Magnum had infused its epic stadium rock with more and more symphonic elements, leaning more often toward the sound of an energized Asia, which made each release more interesting. With its rich sound, finely crafted and catchy melodies, and flawless performance, Magnum came closer than ever to a sophisticated and universal form of heavy prog, quite close to the best of Uriah Heep, another intrepid English veteran. The ambitious *The Serpent Rings* (2020) is a good example of this."Here Comes the Rain" is cut from the same cloth. At first glance, the opening track "Run Into the Shadows," with its unstoppable riff and luminous melody, doesn't seem to represent a major musical shift. Yet hidden deep within this binary music lies a sort of irrepressible despair, a discreet melancholy. And these lyrics, chanted in a thunderous voice, describe our violent world with such darkness that it all seeps into the flashy metal on the surface. This feeling is amply confirmed by the next track, the haunting "Here Comes the Rain," with an even more progressive sound. And what can be said about "Some Kind of Treachery," a heart-wrenching waltz blending symphonic strings and romantic piano?Tony Clarkin once again wrote and composed the entire album but allowed Benton to bring more diversity and boldness to the arrangements (a Hammond organ solo on the boogie-prog track "Bleu Tango," a Moog solo on "Borderline," or classical organ arpeggios on "I Wanna Live," harp-synth sound on "Broken City," and a rhythm-and-blues brass section on "The Seventh Darkness"). Keyboards take center stage ("After the Silence," "Broken City"), while the guitars often remain in the background or provide rhythmic accompaniment, sometimes acoustic ("Here Comes the Rain," "Broken City"). This trend, combined with a greater proportion of slow, melancholic tracks with highly evocative titles (the tragic "Broken City," the anxious "Here Comes the Rain"), and more necessarily binary ones ("Some Kind of Treachery"), where singer Bob Catley?a longtime member of the band whose powerful vocals remain undiminished despite his 76 years?also knows how to be more delicate and moving?all of this makes this dark album more endearing than its predecessors.How can one remain unmoved while listening to "I Wanna Live," with its premonitory undertones, sung with rage by Catley and written by the man who would soon leave this life? I wanna live/ I wanna shout (?) / I wanna live my one desire / Come on and take my hand and walk me through the fire. The magnificent "Borderline," which evokes Rainbow, or even Fish, with its electro-tribal intro and its coda featuring delicate classical piano, brings the flawless *Here Comes the Rain* to a regal close?a bitter and pessimistic swan song, yet one devoid of weakness or clumsiness throughout these fifty memorable minutes.Magnum enjoyed little success in France but great success among our German neighbors, where the majority of their releases reached the top 5 on the sales charts. *Here Comes the Rain* even peaked at No. 2 there upon its release. It is well deserved. After a prolific career, spent largely in the service of a band he could be proud of, Tony Clarkin thus bowed out with what will certainly remain one of Magnum's best albums?an important band worth discovering if you haven't already.

items.body: Düsseldorf and Electronic music have been inextricably linked for decades. The city has produced a distinctive musical legacy in which experimentation, electronics, minimalism, and a fascination with the future have always been central. It is a history that stretches back to the 1970s and 1980s, when electronic music, with Kraftwerk as its pioneering flagship, was not so much regarded as an exercise in nostalgia, but rather as a way of looking towards the future. It was within this tradition that Mängelexemplar emerged in 2011, simply abbreviated as MNGLXMPLR. The Düsseldorf duo, consisting of Lilli B. and Joa Carisma, found their place in the international underground with a distinctive blend of Minimal-Wave and Electro-Pop. Their name — stripped of its vowels to become the almost cryptic MNGLXMPLR — seems perfectly suited to their musical universe: sleek, unconventional, and just a little elusive. Over the years, MNGLXMPLR have established themselves as a familiar name on the scene, performing at numerous festivals and venues both in Germany and abroad. With their new album, “Neue Zukunft,” released this spring on Infacted Recordings, they continue their exploration of Minimal-Wave, delivering an opus that feels darker, harder, and more intense. I spoke with both protagonists about the album, their musical journey, and the future of MNGLXMPLR. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Q: MNGLXMPLR has now been active for more than ten years. Looking back, what are the first thoughts that come to mind? What have been the defining moments or biggest highlights so far, and how would you say the band has evolved over the years? M:More than ten years… that’s quite a statement. The funny thing is, there was never a ten-year plan. We founded MNGLXMPLR because we wanted to make music. One year became five, five became ten – and suddenly here we are. There have been intense phases, quiet phases, great shows, frustrating moments, and countless ideas that never made it anywhere. That’s part of it. The biggest change is probably that we’ve become much more confident in our own musical language. In the beginning, there was more searching and experimenting. Today, we have a much better sense of what feels right for MNGLXMPLR. But we don’t want to turn that into a formula. The moment you know exactly what the next track is going to sound like, things become boring. There have been many highlights over the years – releases, concerts, travels and encounters that happened through the music. But the biggest highlight is actually very simple: we’re still here. And we’re still curious. Q: It took several years for “Neue Zukunft” to finally see the light of day. I imagine that period brought about changes – not only in terms of your studio setup, but also in your songwriting and creative process. Could you tell us a little about how you have evolved and how that development shaped the album? M:“Neue Zukunft” took its time. A lot changed at Carismastudios during those years. The studio evolved, new equipment was added, different projects emerged, and we experimented with different ways of working. Some of those experiments eventually became part of the album. There are tracks that existed for years before they found their final form. We kept coming back to them, changing things, removing things, and sometimes simply leaving them alone for a while. Our songwriting has become more intuitive over time. We don’t sit down and say, ‘Today we’re going to write a minimal track’. A song can start with a beat, a sound, a voice, or simply a certain mood. The emotional side has also become more important. We wanted the emotion to already be present in the music, rather than being added later through production. The result has become harder and more direct in some places, but the minimalist foundation has remained. And we have no problem with a few rough edges. For us, perfect doesn’t automatically mean interesting. Q: What can you tell us about “Neue Zukunft”? What is the central idea or concept behind the album, and how do you look back on the composition, recording and production process today? M:“Neue Zukunft” is about change and movement. It’s not a concept album in the classic sense. There isn’t one single story that you have to decode. It’s more like a collection of different moods and sides of MNGLXMPLR. Minimalist structures, darker atmospheres, harder sounds and emotional moments. We wanted to preserve these contrasts. The visual identity also became an important part of the album. For this, we are working with Düsseldorf fashion icon Ela Holscher, fashion designer Michaela Reinhardt-Beron and photographer Thomas Stelzmann. In Düsseldorf, music, fashion, photography and art have always been closely connected. So for us, this connection felt very natural. But we didn’t want to turn it into nostalgia. We have no interest in pretending it’s 1982 again. Düsseldorf has its history. We’re interested in what we can do with it today. This idea is also carried onto the stage. Sound, visuals, fashion and performance should become part of the same atmosphere. Q: The title “Neue Zukunft” immediately catches the eye – particularly at a time shaped by increasing geopolitical tensions, social uncertainty and war. At the same time, we are entering a new artistic era in which algorithms, AI and digital technologies are increasingly influencing how music is created and consumed. What does the title “Neue Zukunft” mean to you, and how does it reflect your view of the world today? M:We deliberately wanted a title that looks ahead. There is already enough dystopian language around us. Of course, we see what is happening in the world. War, political conflicts and uncertainty are part of the present. But “Neue Zukunft” is not about resignation. It’s about movement. The future is coming anyway. AI is obviously part of that future and is already changing the way music is created and consumed. We don’t use AI to create MNGLXMPLR. For us, the human process remains essential: writing, playing, recording, making mistakes and changing things. Electronic music, however, has always been closely connected to technological change. Synthesizers, samplers and computers changed the way musicians work. AI will be another major shift. We don’t think it makes sense to simply accept it blindly or reject it outright. You have to question it. You have to decide what you want to use from it and why. “Neue Zukunft” doesn’t mean that we know what tomorrow will look like. It means that we’re ready to find out. Q: These days, many listeners focus more on playlists and individual singles than on complete albums. I personally still believe that an album represents a comprehensive artistic statement. Do you think the album format remains relevant in an increasingly fragmented and fast-paced musical landscape? M:Absolutely. A single can work on its own. But an album gives it context. You can build an atmosphere, create tension and connect tracks that might work very differently as individual singles. That’s important to us. “Neue Zukunft” was made as an album, and the sequence of the tracks matters. And then there’s the album on vinyl. We like the physical experience. You take the record out of the sleeve, look at the artwork, put it on and listen. Then you turn it over. You can’t really speed that up. And maybe that’s exactly the point. In a world where everything is instantly available, a record forces you to slow down. You can even hold the music in your hands. Artwork, photography, design and music become one shared object. That still has value. Q: MNGLXMPLR is also very much a live band – you have even played in Belgium three times already. How important are live performances to your identity as a band? How do you transfer the atmosphere of your studio recordings to the stage, and what touring plans do you have in connection with “Neue Zukunft”? M:Playing live is extremely important to us. The studio is controlled; the stage isn’t. That’s exactly why we like it. We don’t want to simply reproduce “Neue Zukunft” live exactly as it sounds on the record. The live versions are more direct, more physical and sometimes even harder. But the atmosphere has to remain intact. The audience also changes the performance. You can prepare a set, but you can’t prepare a room. We’ve already played in Belgium three times, and every concert had its own character. That’s one of the reasons we enjoy playing abroad. With “Neue Zukunft”, we want to play a new series of concerts across Europe. Looking towards 2027, we also want to move beyond the classic minimal scene, discover other Electronic scenes and play larger stages. The visual side will also become more important. Not as decoration, but as part of the performance. Sound, light, fashion, photography and movement should belong together. We don’t want people to simply hear “Neue Zukunft”. We want them to experience it. Q: You come from Düsseldorf, a city that will forever be associated with KRAFTWERK. To what extent do you still feel this artistic legacy among Electronic artists from the city today? Has Düsseldorf’s musical heritage directly or indirectly influenced your own work? M:Kraftwerk is unavoidable. If you make Electronic music in Düsseldorf, you grow up with that history. But Düsseldorf is much more than Kraftwerk. DAF, Die Krupps and many other artists developed completely different forms of electronic music. What connects them for us isn’t necessarily a particular sound. It’s an attitude: experimenting, reducing, making music physical, questioning things, and not caring too much whether someone has already invented a genre for it. We can relate to that a lot. But we don’t want to sound like Kraftwerk, or DAF, or Die Krupps. They’ve already done that – and pretty well. So our connection to Düsseldorf’s musical history is more indirect. You grow up surrounded by music, art, fashion, photography and clubs. You absorb that environment without necessarily realizing it. And years later, you realize how much of it has stayed with you. So yes, Düsseldorf has influenced MNGLXMPLR. But we don’t want to become a heritage band. We respect the past, but musically, we live in the here and now. Look back. Take with you what matters. Keep moving forward.

items.body: Kommission Z80 is a Swedish duo that, following a debut album released on Electric Underground Records, is now self-releasing its second opus. I don’t recall ever hearing anything by them before, but these 13 tracks provide a clear picture of the duo’s musical identity. Their primary influences clearly lie within the realm of old-school EBM—specifically the kind of EBM characterized by thoughtful composition and well-crafted arrangements. The vocals, and indeed some of the tracks, remind me somewhat of Portion Control, while other songs reveal traces of Skinny Puppy’s influence. One track even feels like a nod to Front 242. It should be noted that these are all bands with highly distinctive sounds and complex structures. Kommission Z80 doesn’t quite reach that level yet; they would benefit from improving some technical aspects, particularly the mixing and recording. Nevertheless, there is undeniable potential here. Several strong tracks are waiting to be discovered, and the latter part of the album, in particular, features some very cool songs. Kommission Z80 is a name that true EBM enthusiasts should remember. (Rating:7). items.body: I went to bed I saw you there You shook your head It’s all out, where? There is a special cruelty in being wounded by someone who has already left the room. The accusation lands, the door closes, and suddenly one person possesses the luxury of departure while the other inherits everything that remains unresolved. They replay every sentence, defend themselves to an empty room, and search for the words they were never allowed to speak. Kind Kid’s latest single bleed inhabits precisely that imbalance, turning abandonment into a bright, brisk synthpop song whose surface seems almost indecently cheerful beside the injury underneath. The arrangement draws its movement from eighties synthpop and its darker hues from the gothic electronics of Clan of Xymox to the Modern Darkwave sensibilities of Boy Harsher, with eerie synth flourishes and cold, uneasy tones curling around a dark disco beat. The rhythm keeps the song moving toward the dance floor, though something in those keyboards suggests the argument will be waiting when you get home. Julien Martinez sings from the position of someone denied the final word, his sense of injury finding an accomplice in the music’s disquiet. That tension gives “bleed” its emotional force: the hooks offer release while the synths keep returning to the bruise. The lyrics are deliberately circular. Images return, phrases repeat, and the speaker seems trapped inside an encounter that has ended everywhere except in his own mind. Repetition becomes psychological rather than decorative, suggesting those arguments one continues hours later while washing dishes, driving home, or staring at the ceiling, inventing increasingly perfect replies for someone who is no longer listening. “I thought of it as some metaphorical situation where someone’s been left behind after some sort of attack… left to “bleed,” muses Kind Kid frontman Julien Martinez. “Sometimes a situation can feel so much different to one person than the other.” One person may regard an argument as a momentary discharge of anger; the other can experience the same exchange as an injury requiring days to understand. bleed catches that disparity without weighing down its pop architecture. Its hooks remain airy, almost playful, while the words circle rejection, exposure, and helplessness. items.body: Are we better off alone Will I come into my own Are we better off alone Being understood by someone is a comfort until the relationship ends and their imagined opinion starts conducting an inspection of everything wrong with you. Boy Harsher’s Faulty inhabits that uncomfortable interval between asking to be wanted and wondering what that wanting has cost. Jae Matthews sings as though the verdict may already be in, while Augustus Muller gives her doubts enough room to move. The question of being better off alone becomes something to turn over on the dancefloor, where thinking clearly has always been optional. The song accompanies the release of Get Mean, out now following its September 18 arrival through Atlantic Records. Their first album since 2022’s The Runner, the twelve-track record follows the end of Matthews and Muller’s romantic relationship in early 2024, after a period of family loss, personal upheaval, and creative uncertainty. Continuing the band meant finding a way to work together while the terms of their lives were changing. That makes the tenderness of Faulty particularly affecting: the people making this music understand how complicated its questions can become. A kicking beat, busy hi-hats, and quivering synths set Faulty in motion. Its dark disco rhythm has some of Careful’s physical insistence, softened by broad synth pads and little descending electronic notes that drop through the arrangement with a rounded, almost playful boop. When the beat pauses to breathe, the synths take on a Vangelis-like warble, briefly opening the song into something more spacious and cinematic. The rhythm returns beneath a lead synth that bends up and down in pitch, while Matthews keeps her voice hushed and close, breathing the words with a tenderness that borders on resignation. The lyrics put affection and self-assessment in an uncomfortable room together. Asking whether she is faulty gives another person the power to diagnose her; asking whether she will come into her own begins to take some of that power back. Repetition keeps either possibility from becoming a settled conclusion. Matthews sounds caught between wanting to be held and recognizing how much of herself might be waiting outside the relationship. Directed by Boy Harsher and shot on 35mm with cinematography by Owen Smith-Clark, the final video in the Get Mean series returns to a room lined in brown wood paneling. A television glows blue on a black stand, a small fan sits by the window, and a microphone cable trails across the carpet. Against that ordinary setting, the changing cast look dressed for entirely different evenings: a white cowboy hat, metallic bodysuits, striped knitwear, black boots. Each person seems to have brought a private version of the same bad night. The camera moves from fixed views of the room into close-ups of faces, hands, and bodies moving past one another. People share the frame, lean together, or briefly touch, but proximity never quite settles the question in the chorus. There is a lovely awkwardness to it: the self-consciousness of dancing at home, followed by the sudden absorption of forgetting you are being watched. By the end, the people have gone and the television is still there. The room has held all that feeling without offering anyone an answer. Watch the video for Faulty below: Across Get Mean, the effort to keep going takes several musical forms. Writing began to move again when Matthews took to the road, travelling through West Texas, the Pacific Northwest, and South Florida. The album was eventually recorded in eight locations across the United States, Mexico, and Italy, its unsettled circumstances allowing new sounds and approaches into the duo’s work. Matthews describes it as “what I had to give during the most extreme period of my life.” The three singles we covered ahead of its release made clear how much that offering could contain. The first indication came with Jeans, released in June. Its springy guitar figure and bubbling electronics brought a new wave directness to Boy Harsher, with a steel-slide twang giving the song a western accent. Our earlier comparison to the Pretenders still fits the way Matthews’ cool delivery rides that guitar, while the buoyancy also suggests Muller’s work in Safe Mind. Beneath the cheek is a sharp little study of ambition: the dream of escaping a small town, the dream of becoming somebody, and the possibility of ending up selling an image of freedom by the pair. The band’s latex line-dancing video, conceived with Robert Palmer’s Addicted to Love in mind, makes that collision between aspiration, performance, and merchandise deliciously literal. Hard Beat, unveiled alongside July’s album announcement, tightens the pressure around a repeating bass-synth figure and an unrelenting kick. As we noted then, there is something of Depeche Mode’s Behind the Wheel in its meeting of motion, desire, and surrendered control. Matthews moves between confession and invitation while the rhythm keeps pushing ahead. Its video makes those exchanges physical through an elaborate leg brace, a Cadillac, and a handheld camcorder, drawing medical hardware, automotive controls, and the invasive act of filming into the same uneasy visual language. Within the album, the track preserves the severe club momentum that has long served Boy Harsher so well, giving the softer and more openly melodic songs something solid to push against. August’s Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call) puts a warmer arrangement around the indignity of waiting for someone to remember you exist. A brisk new wave beat, rounded bass, bright keyboards, and short bursts of distorted guitar carry Matthews’ unhappy drawl toward the sort of pop chorus that can make despair briefly feel sociable. Her insistence that she is okay sounds increasingly like something she needs to practice. Our earlier review followed that idea into the lyric video, where yellow karaoke lettering crosses the blue screen of a CRT television. Created with vintage video equipment by Sean McGuirk and shot by Jesse Korman, it turns failed communication into a singalong with nobody else visibly present. Heard beside Faulty, the song makes the eventual question of solitude feel earned. Coming Home opens with Matthews in a smoky, Lynchian register, her voice suspended over steadily repeating synths and a breezy dance beat. The low guitar tones bring New Order to mind, with the melodic weight of a Peter Hook bassline translated onto guitar. That combination gives the song an appealing pull between bodily ease and emotional uncertainty. The rhythm leaves the windows open; the vocal suggests someone still deciding whether it is safe to come inside. Here, the album’s broader musical interests allow vulnerability to sound inviting without making it seem simple. Ice Pick (Walk Away) makes a particularly satisfying turn toward gothic rock. The parenthetical invites a Sisters of Mercy comparison before the guitar has even had its say, and the melody strengthens the association with their First and Last and Always period. A deep post-punk bass groove and the crunchy splash of the drum machine give the track a familiar dry ice chill. Matthews’ tender delivery moderates that severity, placing a vulnerable voice inside an arrangement with its collar firmly turned up. The resemblance is a pleasure to hear, especially from a duo whose love of this music has often been expressed through a different set of instruments. Pray 4 Me lets the bass loosen its hips. Soft synth pads, a sexy funk groove, and quivering bell tones bring a strain of Bryan Ferry-eque sophisti-pop into the album, expanding its capacity for pleasure as well as distress. There is a suppleness to the arrangement that makes this feel like a natural extension of the record’s emotional dynamic range. Desire, after all, does not become less complicated when somebody gives it a particularly good bassline. Boy Harsher sounds comfortable letting elegance and appetite share the same song. The album closes with Bleed, setting trip-hop beats against crystalline synths and low, bone-marrow-churning bass. Imagine the Bristol-born genre taking shape inside the electric dreams of the mid-1980s: the drums with a twitching hi-hat and thump have that low, unhurried weight, while the electronics give the space around them a cool, glassy clarity. After the movement of the preceding songs, this slower finish lets the record exhale. Its change of pace offers a place to sit with everything that has happened. Get Mean gives Matthews and Muller’s affection for post-punk, synthpop, goth, and dance music considerably more room to misbehave. They have grown as people, their lives have changed, and their music has had the good sense to evolve. Those expecting Pain on an endless loop, or Careful with a fresh set of track titles, may find this development inconvenient. For listeners who share Jae and Gus’s musical curiosity, there is pleasure in hearing them loosen up, follow their enthusiasms, and discover what this new chapter of their partnership can become. And if Get Mean isn’t the Boy Harsher you ordered, well, tough shit. Listen to Get Mean below and order the album here. Additional listening and purchase options are available here. Their background in film became central to 2022’s The Runner, which they wrote, produced, directed, and scored. Their work in cinema also includes The Lonely Woman, their debut feature as directors, starring Chloë Sevigny, FKA twigs, and Sturgill Simpson. items.body: ケイシー・カンジェローシ 初来日リサイタルに寄せて 世界中のパーカッショニストを魅了する演奏家・作曲家、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。その初来日リサイタルが、2026年9月26日（土）、長久手市文化の家 森のホール（愛知県）で開催される。公演に寄せられた3人のコメントと映像から、その魅力を紹介する。 打楽器音楽の常識を覆す発想 新野将之（マルチパーカッショニスト） 僕が最も敬愛する打楽器奏者、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。 彼の音楽には、「打楽器でここまでできるのか！」という驚きが詰まっています。卓越したテクニックはもちろん、タンバリンやスネアドラムの可能性を極限まで追求し、石を打ち合わせる音、電子音、パントマイムまで音楽の中へ大胆に取り込んでしまう。その発想は、まさに打楽器音楽の常識を覆すものです。 そして何より面白いのは、彼の音楽が「聴く」だけでは終わらないこと。音、身体、動き、空間……すべてをひとつの表現として融合させ、クラシック音楽の枠を飛び越え、新しいエンターテイメントへと昇華させていきます。 アートでありながら、圧倒的に楽しい。 知的でありながら、魂を揺さぶる。 打楽器の未来を切り拓いてきた開拓者、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。その唯一無二の世界を、ぜひ生で体感してください！ ﻿ 身体表現と、超絶技巧の打楽器演奏を一体化 小室敬幸（音楽ライター） 1982年にアメリカで生まれたケイシー・カンジェローシは、打楽器を音だけでなく、奏者の身体や身振りまで含む舞台表現として捉えているユニークな打楽器奏者で作曲家だ。今回のリサイタルで演奏されるティエリー・ドゥ・メイ《Silence Must Be!》は、その志向を象徴する選曲である。メイはローザスを率いるアンヌ・テレサ・ドゥ・ケースマイケルら、ベルギーのコンテンポラリーダンスと密接に活動し、音楽的にはルイ・アンドリーセンらに連なるヨーロッパ的なミニマリズムを結びつけた作曲家。そのメイのような音楽の系譜に位置づけられるカンジェローシは、代表作《Meditation No.1》を含む自身の作品でも、打つ、振る、構えるといった動作や反復が、音と同じほど重要な表現になる。ダンスや演劇に通じる身体表現と、超絶技巧の打楽器演奏を一体化させており、今や世界中の若いパーカショニストを魅了している作曲家なのだ。目で見て真価が味わえる音楽なので、日本で初めて行う本格的リサイタルは必聴・必見である！ フィクションとフィジカルのあわい 加藤綾子（ヴァイオリニスト） YouTubeやInstagram上で切り抜かれる、カンジェローシの身体。バストアップであったり、手元や指先であったりするそれらを画面越しに見たとき、わたしたちは、まずそのディテールに心を奪われる。その身体は多彩な楽器を、ごく当たり前に扱う（ように見える）。ティエリー・ドゥ・メイのスコアを、美しく実現する。石ころもオルゴールも、スティックも、あまりに自然に振る舞うものだから、まるでオブジェクト・シアターを鑑賞しているような感覚に陥る。 そのうえで、彼は切実な演奏者であり続ける。鍛錬された身振りは、どこまでいっても彼自身あるいは他者の音楽を実践し、批評するためにある。その切実さが、きっと、ひとびとの全身を鷲掴む。画面越しではない、実存として長久手に立つ「カンジェローシ」は、音楽というフィクションとフィジカルのあわいを鮮やかに描き、突きつけてくれるだろう。──つまり、生で見るカンジェローシの演奏は、めっちゃすごくてやばいはず、ということです。 公演情報 ケイシー・カンジェローシ パーカッションリサイタル TENDRILS 2026年9月26日（土）16:00 長久手市文化の家 森のホール（愛知県） 公演詳細：https://bunkanoie.jp/archives/9250

items.body: Richard J. Birkin’s official soundtrack to Jon McGregor’s Reservoir 13 was written, performed, and recorded live with Haiku Salut, an instrumental trio from the English Midlands. The book was awarded the 2017 COSTA Novel of the Year, and its soundtrack wears the same shoes; its blue threads help in framing a photograph of sudden loneliness, its strings wrapped up in midwinter mystery. Described by The Guardian as ‘a chilling meditation on loss and time’, Reservoir 13’s soundtrack is equally cool-blooded. The strings search for missing 13-year-old Rebecca, the sudden loss of light shrivelling the music into a sluggish state of shock. The unexplained and instantaneous earthquake, an event as cataclysmic as the one in Don DeLillo’s Point Omega, sends an endless ripple through tomorrow. Everyone’s looking for answers – crime or no crime – but life doesn’t work like that; the Universe isn’t required to offer a neat resolution or a form of closure. For the most part, things drift. People drift. Unexpected, and often terrible, events happen each and every day. Threads often just run out, with no explanation given, and no end to suffering in sight. No resolving. But, for Birkin, this is potent material. Strings swell slowly, and that gives the music more of an edge. Paradoxically, an unstoppable force, screaming at the top of its lungs, can be felt inside the quiet, caressing motion of the bow. A muted scream. Whenever McGregor was at a book reading, Birkin’s technology allowed the writer access to the phones in the audience, creating a communal experience as the reciting of words, along with an unfolding section of the story, met with audience participation – and, of course, this produced a number of different outcomes. Not one reading was ever the same. The piano has always lent itself to deep pools of thought and sliding melancholia, but in this case it’s gut-wrenching, less a sole tear or an escaping trickle from the eye and more an inconsolable aching. The music disappears, too. Physically present but mentally gone, haunted by an ongoing and incredibly traumatic event, the music seems to be preoccupied with this all-consuming grief, hardly able to process pain as the crushing weight of the strings continue to bear down upon the creaking stave. The residents are trapped in a horrific situation, and the melody can’t find a way to break out of its minor key, either. The single piano motif is important, as it seems to represent isolation, a singular sorrow, a loneliness and an inability to do anything about anything. Later, strings join the search party, weeping along with the piano. Life has to go on, but a sick mood hangs over the land. The soundtrack is heavy, but that only makes it all the more powerful. Soundtracks are often only reserved for film, although listeners have, in the past, been blessed with book-scores, like those in The Book Report series, so this somewhat novel (excuse me) approach is an area that can be further explored. Film will always offer strict representations and the forced digestion of its images, while the book is individual, creating its own imagery for every reader. The reader has to work in order to create the world. Likewise, music is subjective, too, but the book’s theme ensures sober music. The book’s meditation on loss requires a deep sensitivity, and Birkin ushers the strings to appropriate, and respectful, places, the piano gently bleeding from its emotional wounds. www.rjbirkin.bandcamp.com

items.body: Olivier Alary’s compositions are draped over a misty scattering of naked trees. The season could be late autumn instead of early spring. Fiction / Non-Fiction is a collection of the composer’s film soundtrack work, which is imbued with a haunting atmosphere and a broad range of instrumentation. Accordion, saxophone, slide guitar, vibraphone, marimba, guitar, gongs, electronics, flute, double bass, clarinet and choir are all used, highlighting in marker pen a desire to give the music as full a life as possible. Remarkably, Fiction / Non-Fiction feels cohesive and surprisingly sparse when it could so easily have been cluttered. Slightly strange melodies slowly creep outside, moving from shadows into light, limping at a slanted angle which in turn gives the record a darkly unique sound. They sway as if in the middle of a tribal dance which to outsiders appears utterly alien. For the most part, the music is balletic and somewhat downtrodden, with a weak glow that is all but ready to fizzle out. Alary brings something fresh to an overpopulated genre, with the music becoming a bronze sunflower encircled by a growing number of weeds. A deep maturity rises like smoke from its slow vapours, echoing A Winged Victory for the Sullen or Stars of the Lid, lifting it up above the common. The composer has chosen to push the music beyond, embracing possibilities with an illimitable sound like that of evolution, carrying on its back a completely engaging and captivating style unlike anything else. A sliver of chrome light leaks out from the strings before trickling into the piano’s pool of flowing liquid. The pieces all flow as one, despite the album being labelled a collection. Its cool flavours give the album an original aftertaste. The smooth saxophone recedes into a fragile shell, becoming a paler, washed-out thing – as if it had just encountered a vampire – while its sultry colour leaks from every note, and the flute whispers over a tired breath of wind. The Montreal-based Frenchman, who has previously collaborated with Bjork, delivers a poetic album comprised of contemplative and deeply expressive composition. Rainy thoughts splash down onto the ground, and strings are soaked in grey hues. While the differing instruments naturally add colour to the album, it’s always pale and almost absent, tertiary and not primary. Fiction / Non-Fiction has a round form and gilded edges, but its inner space is dressed in an eternal shade of grey. www.130701.com

items.body: Long Story Short Dosed up on pretty high levels of reverb, Long Story Short is glistening, translucent music. Rain lightly falls as the bass note of an electric guitar sets the first stone in place. After that, soft sprinklings of notes are swept away on the perfumed, lilting air of major seventh chords. Appropriately titled ‘Lazing’, the music drifts by, seamlessly adding a little at a time. Like a cloud in the sky, it takes its time to fully form. Released on Too Many Fireworks, the ambient guitar music of Mateusz Franczak is sweet and soothing, at times lively and slightly frantic (which is unusual for the style of ambient guitar) without ever sounding cluttered, and at other times radiating a depthless serenity that ripples along with the reverb. The Polish experimental musician layers his ambient music with kindness, but there’s also a distorted, uneasy and thoroughly grey undercurrent in the depths of the ambient sound. That’s a mean feat in itself, because ambient music so often relies on its sparse vacuums that occupy the no-man’s-land between space and silence. The distorted intruder doesn’t dampen the slow, slightly melancholic feel, either. The notes ring and bleed together; the double stops clang with a muted tone that drags everything into a murky field of vision. A calming, casual tone captains the largely sedate music, its notes dimmed like the fine evening light of late spring. The shadows lurk just around the corner and are a couple of hours away from arriving, but as long as the music’s playing they never dare to creep out of their dark shells. A grittier sound sticks tightly to ‘Moving’. The prickly distortion is there, but it’s not strong enough to dampen the sound as a whole. The faces in the crowd appear to be crisper and sharper. Long Story Short takes a stride towards ambient song, too, the vocals gliding into a mini chorus that glows with the fiery heat of napalm. It gets its energy from both the soaring vocal and the spikier tone. Long Story Short lingers between structured song and improvised, sustaining soundscape, blearily straddling the ethereal and the everyday. Emerging out of this is a voice dripping with reverb, recalling the late Spacemen 3 and early Spritualized sound by way of a muddied, soulful drawl. The softer pools of a glorious, romanticized reverb evaporate in the light of a distorted tone that waddles out of the music’s swampy waters like a primeval crocodile. Paradise slips away and is replaced by the heady turbulence of uncertainty and doubt. The faith isn’t as strong as it was; the music’s glow is waning and swaying. Long Story Short is easily digestible, its colourful music as lulling as it is pressing. To a degree, Franczak’s history (he played in a number of rock and punk bands at an earlier age) influences the music’s lifeline, especially when it comes to the use of overdrive. It was, perhaps, inevitable, but it puts a different spin on the music. You get the feeling that Franczak really enjoyed the process. Long Story Short’s largely improvised, intoxicated melodies form a pleasant hybrid, where abrasive textures and passionate vocals blend in with ambient’s gentle curves. www.mateuszfranczak.bandcamp.com
